Worlds That Stayed With Me

Caelan Redekopp

  1. Flavia de Luce
  2. Artemis Fowl
  3. The Unwanteds
  4. Spirited Away
  5. Everything Everywhere All at Once
  6. Actual Life (April 14 – December 17 2020)

Flavia de Luce

Alan Bradley

The first Flavia de Luce books stayed with me because of a feeling I have not quite found in anything else. In The Sweetness at the Bottom of the Pie, the excitement of the mystery exists alongside a strange loneliness, with Flavia disconnected from her family in a massive house that feels mostly empty. Her curiosity and knowledge of chemistry make the story exciting, but they do not seem to remove that distance between her and the people around her. I think that contrast is part of what made the books feel so intense: I could be caught up in an extraordinary mystery and still feel that underlying solitude. I remember The Weed That Strings the Hangman’s Bag being especially overwhelming near its climax, with Flavia using pigeon droppings to make an antidote for someone poisoned with cyanide. The way her knowledge became useful in such an unlikely situation made the scene feel almost impossible. I read the first three books together in one enormous volume, which was an experience in itself. Getting through something that looked so daunting taught me that I could make progress on a task that initially seemed ridiculous to attempt.

Artemis Fowl

Eoin Colfer

The Artemis Fowl series was a fundamental part of my childhood, especially the first book and The Last Guardian. I listened to the whole series so many times that returning to it became almost meditative. The pacing was a large part of that, because the stories could be exciting while still feeling familiar enough for me to settle into them. I connected with the characters, and the worldbuilding made the world feel much larger than the part of it I could see. One detail I still remember distinctly from the series is Taipei 101 and learning about its mass damper through a story taking place there. Having something so extraordinary happen in a real location made the invented world feel connected to the one I lived in, rather than entirely separate from it. The series gave me both the excitement of discovering something unfamiliar and the comfort of returning to something I knew.

The Unwanteds

Lisa McMann

What fascinated me about The Unwanteds was how completely a story could change my understanding of the world it had introduced. It begins in a bleak society where being sent away seems to mean that a character’s life is over, so the discovery of another possibility changes the meaning of everything that came before it. I found it interesting that someone could grow up believing they understood the limits of their world, while having no idea what existed beyond them. The connection between art and magic was also incredibly compelling to me, especially the idea that something like origami could become a magical tool. Creativity was not just something characters enjoyed; it could change what they were able to do. That made the contrast with the dullness of the world at the beginning feel even stronger. Looking back, I can see how much I liked stories that revealed a hidden world, but this one stood out because imagination and making things were part of what made that world possible.

Spirited Away

Hayao Miyazaki

Spirited Away is one of my favourite works of art, although it is difficult to explain exactly why it means so much to me. Its worldbuilding is incredible, but unlike many of the books I loved as a child, that is not the main thing I remember loving about it. What matters most to me is the emotional feeling underneath Chihiro’s journey. The art and music do not feel separate from that story; they are part of what makes the experience so powerful. I can admire how carefully the world has been created, while also feeling something that I cannot fully explain by listing the things happening in it. That is part of why the film stays with me rather than just being something I thought was impressive when I watched it. It showed me how strongly a work can affect me even when I cannot put that response neatly into words.

Everything Everywhere All at Once

Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert

Everything Everywhere All at Once feels like an almost impossibly wild journey, yet what stayed with me was how human it becomes. So much of the movie is absurd, and its constant changes make it feel as though there might not be any stable way to understand what is happening. But instead of making the relationships seem insignificant beside all those possibilities, the film makes them feel more important. I found that incredibly moving, because the emotional centre is not an explanation that suddenly makes the universe sensible. It is the connection between people, even when everything around them is difficult to make sense of. The contrast between the scale of the movie and the intimacy of what matters in the end is a large part of why it made me cry. It connects with my sense that, even if everything else is absurd, our humanity and our relationships can still matter.

Actual Life (April 14 – December 17 2020)

Fred again..

The Actual Life series has had a large impact on me, and the first album captures much of what I find so distinctive about Fred again..’s music. I connect it with the isolation of COVID, but also with people reaching for one another and speaking about things they are struggling with. The way voices and fragments of life are built into the music makes it feel unusually human to me. They are not just words placed over a finished piece of music; they help give the music its shape and emotional meaning. I think that is part of why it feels so different from simply listening to someone describe an emotion in a song. There is a sense of being allowed into pieces of other people’s lives, even though those pieces have been transformed into something new. Like the films that have affected me most, it brings me back to connection, but it does so through sound rather than a conventional story.
